findings.title: Issuer (iss) allow-list bypass via array claim loose match
findings.evidence: Root cause: validateClaimValues() at src/verifier.js:159 uses an existential test, `if (!values.some(v => allowed.some(a => a.test(v))))`, so a string claim passes if ANY one of its values matches the allow-list. verifyToken() (lines 208-227) turns any array-valued claim into `values` (line 211-212) and calls validateClaimValues() for every non-date claim, regardless of the validator's `array` flag (line 226); validateClaimType() (lines 144-151) only checks that each element is a string, so it never rejects an array for a single-valued claim. The `iss` validator is registered at lines 474-475 without `array: true` and without strict handling. Reachability: an attacker submits a signed JWT whose payload contains `"iss": ["https://evil.example", "https://trusted.example"]` (or even `["https://trusted.example"]`). decode() yields the array; verifyToken computes arrayValue=true/values=the array; validateClaimType passes because every element is a string; validateClaimValues' `.some(...)` returns true because the trusted issuer is present, so the token is accepted as if it were issued by the trusted issuer. This spoofs the issuer identity and defeats the allowedIss access-control check (CWE-290). The same loose-match flaw also affects the other non-array string claims (jti/sub/nonce), but iss is the demonstrated reachable path.
